o: A window is valid when at most k distinct values occur more than once inside it. Track value counts plus a running count 'rep' of values whose count is exactly ≥ 2; expand the right end, and whenever rep exceeds k shrink from the left until valid again. Both pointers only move forward, giving linear time. Example 1: window [2,3,1,2,3,4] has repeating values {2,3}, exactly k = 2, length 6.
k: Maintain cnt[v] and rep = number of values with cnt ≥ 2; validity is rep ≤ k.
Increment rep when a count hits 2; decrement when it falls back to 1.
Amortized two-pointer movement gives O(n) total.

a.n: Approach 1: Sliding window with repetition counter
a.i: Classic variable-size window: extend r, update counts/rep, then advance l while rep > k. Record r − l + 1 after each restoration of validity.
s: For each r: cnt[nums[r]]++; if it became 2, rep++.
While rep > k: decrement cnt[nums[l]], lowering rep if a count drops to 1, l++.

c.python:
from collections import defaultdict
class Solution:
    def longestSemiRepeatingSubarray(self, nums, k):
        cnt = defaultdict(int)
        rep = l = ans = 0
        for r, x in enumerate(nums):
            cnt[x] += 1
            if cnt[x] == 2: rep += 1
            while rep > k:
                y = nums[l]
                cnt[y] -= 1
                if cnt[y] == 1: rep -= 1
                l += 1
            ans = max(ans, r - l + 1)
        return ans

a.t: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the window once
a.sp: O(n) for the count map in the worst case

a.n: Approach 2: Binary search on the answer
a.i: Validity is monotone: if a window of length L is valid, every shorter one is too. Binary search L over [1, n]; each check slides a fixed-size window counting values with count ≥ 2 in O(n). Total O(n log n) — slower than two pointers but a robust template when the predicate is trickier to maintain incrementally.
s: Binary search the largest valid length L.
check(L): slide a window of size L with a count map and rep counter.
Return the largest L passing the check.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def longestSemiRepeatingSubarray(self, nums, k):
        from collections import Counter
        def ok(L):
            c = Counter(nums[:L])
            rep = sum(1 for v in c.values() if v >= 2)
            if rep <= k: return True
            for r in range(L, len(nums)):
                c[nums[r]] += 1
                if c[nums[r]] == 2: rep += 1
                c[nums[r-L]] -= 1
                if c[nums[r-L]] == 1: rep -= 1
                if rep <= k: return True
            return False
        lo, hi, ans = 1, len(nums), 1
        while lo <= hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if ok(mid): ans, lo = mid, mid + 1
            else: hi = mid - 1
        return ans

a.t: O(n log n) — log n binary-search rounds, each an O(n) window scan

w: Default to the sliding window — it is optimal and simple. Pitfalls: misreading 'k elements repeat' as 'k duplicate occurrences' (it is k distinct values with multiplicity ≥ 2), and forgetting k = 0 forces all-distinct windows. Follow-up: at most k total duplicate occurrences instead of k repeated values (track surplus = Σ(cnt−1) instead).
